prompt: While `done >= planned` is false, what happens to the paragraph inside the `@if` block?

choices.text: It stays in the page, hidden with `display: none`
choices.why: That is what `[hidden]` would do. `@if` takes it out of the page.

choices.text: It does not exist in the page
choices.why: Right. `--html` showed only the `@else` paragraph.

choices.text: It is drawn empty, as a placeholder for later
choices.why: Nothing is drawn; there is only a comment marking the place.

choices.text: It is drawn and then removed after the first check
choices.why: It is never drawn while the condition is false.

prompt: `look --html` showed `<!--container-->` in the summary's HTML. What is it?

choices.text: An element Angular wraps every block in
choices.why: It is a comment, not an element, and nothing is drawn for it.

choices.text: A comment marking where a block's content goes
choices.why: Right. It is Angular's bookmark, and the browser ignores it.

choices.text: The `@else` branch, drawn empty
choices.why: The `@else` branch was drawn as a paragraph with text.

choices.text: A leftover of the HTML comment that names the file
choices.why: The build drops those; this one is Angular's own.

prompt: In `@if (next(); as session) { … }`, why can the block read `session.minutes` without the compiler complaining?

choices.text: `as` converts the value to `any`
choices.why: `as` here names the value; it does not change its type to `any`.

choices.text: Templates are not type-checked inside blocks
choices.why: They are, which is why the narrowing matters.

choices.text: Inside the block, `session` is narrowed to not missing
choices.why: Right. As `if (next)` narrowed it in TypeScript.

choices.text: `next()` never returns `undefined`
choices.why: If it could not, the `@if` would be pointless; it may return nothing.

prompt: What happens if you write `@for (course of courses) { … }` with no `track`?

choices.text: The template does not compile
choices.why: Right. `track` is required.

choices.text: Angular tracks by `$index` for you
choices.why: There is no default; leaving it out is an error.

choices.text: Angular tracks by the item itself, like the old `*ngFor`
choices.why: That was the old directive's behaviour; `@for` refuses instead.

choices.text: It works, with a warning in the console
choices.why: It fails at build time, not at run time.

prompt: Why does the week's course list have an `@empty` block?

choices.text: `@for` requires one, as it requires `track`
choices.why: Only `track` is required.

choices.text: To show a loading message while the courses arrive
choices.why: `@empty` is drawn when the list has no items, which is not the same as loading.

choices.text: So a list with no items still says something
choices.why: Right. Every list starts empty, and that state is the one most often forgotten.

choices.text: To stop the `<ul>` being empty, which is invalid HTML
choices.why: The lesson's reason is the person reading, not validity.

prompt: Match each name `@for` offers with what it is.

pairs.right: whether this is the first item

prompt: After `Reverse`, the 25 typed into the Git row of the list tracked by position appeared next to HTML and CSS. Why?

choices.text: The reverse shuffled the inputs' values on purpose
choices.why: Nothing touched the values; the rows' DOM stayed where it was.

choices.text: Position 2 still existed, so Angular kept that row's DOM and only changed its text
choices.why: Right. The key was the position, and positions do not move.

choices.text: `$index` is computed after the list is drawn
choices.why: When it is computed is not the issue; what it identifies is.

choices.text: jsdom does not keep input values
choices.why: This ran in Chromium, and the other list kept its value correctly.

prompt: A list of sessions is rebuilt from every server answer, with new objects each time. Which track key keeps what the user typed attached to the right session?

choices.text: `track session`, the object itself
choices.why: Every answer brings new objects, so none is recognised and every row is drawn again.

choices.text: `track $index`
choices.why: Positions survive a rebuild, but a reorder moves the data under them.

choices.text: `track session.id`
choices.why: Right. The id survives the rebuild and identifies the session.

choices.text: `track session.date`, since a date is unique
choices.why: Two sessions can share a date, and a date can be edited.

prompt: In the list tracked by `course.id`, what did Angular do with the Git row when the list was reversed?

choices.text: Drew a new row for Git at the top and deleted the old one
choices.why: Then the 25 would have been lost; it moved with the row.

choices.text: Left it in place and changed its text to HTML and CSS
choices.why: That is what happened in the list tracked by position.

choices.text: Moved its existing DOM, field and all, to the top
choices.why: Right. It found the key `git` again.

choices.text: Nothing until the page was reloaded
choices.why: The look ran in one page load, and the row moved.

prompt: `status` is `'done'`. Which of these `@case` lines matches it?

choices.text: `@case ('Done')`
choices.why: Matching uses `===`, and case matters.

choices.text: `@case ('done')`
choices.why: Right. Exactly equal, with `===`.

choices.text: `@case (done)`
choices.why: Without quotes it reads a field called `done`, not the string.

choices.text: `@case ('done' || 'missed')`
choices.why: That expression evaluates to `'done'` and would match by accident, and it reads as two cases.

prompt: With `@default never;`, the build failed with `Type '"planned"' is not assignable to type 'never'`. What was the compiler telling you?

choices.text: That `'planned'` is not a valid status
choices.why: It is valid; the type `Status` lists it.

choices.text: That `never` cannot be used in templates
choices.why: It can; that is how the check works.

choices.text: A status the type allows has no case
choices.why: Right. Every value of `Status` needs its own case once the default says `never`.

choices.text: That `status` was never set
choices.why: It was set to `'missed'`; the check is about the cases, not the value.

prompt: To make a `@switch` fail the build when a value of its type has no case, its default is written `@default ___;`.
Which of these may the template do with `@let left = planned - done;`?

choices.text: Assign to it in an event binding, `(click)="left = 0"`
choices.why: `@let` is read-only, even in an event binding.

choices.text: Read it in a paragraph above the `@let` line
choices.why: It is visible only after its line.

choices.text: Read it in an `@if` below it
choices.why: Right. It is visible after its line and inside the blocks that follow.

choices.text: Read it from the class as `this.left`
choices.why: It belongs to the template; the class does not see it.

prompt: `planned` changes from 165 to 200 while the page is open. What is `left` the next time the template is checked?

choices.text: 75, because `@let` is computed once
choices.why: It is recomputed on every check.
Right. It is recomputed from the values it reads.

choices.text: An error, because `@let` cannot follow a changing value
choices.why: It follows it; it is never stale.

choices.text: 200, the new value of `planned`
choices.why: `left` is `planned - done`, so 200 minus 90.

prompt: A value is needed by the template and by a method of the class, and it takes some work to compute. Where does the lesson say it belongs?

choices.text: In a `@let`, because templates are faster
choices.why: The class cannot read a `@let`.

choices.text: In two `@let` lines, one per use
choices.why: The method would still not see it.

choices.text: In the class, as a `computed` from lesson 6
choices.why: Right. Where the class can use it and a test can check it.

choices.text: In the HTML file, as a comment
choices.why: A comment computes nothing.

prompt: Why did the old `*ngIf` need a separate `<ng-template #none>` for its `else`?

choices.text: The `else` had to be a template the directive could draw or not
choices.why: Right. The `*` wraps an element in a template, and the else needed one too.

choices.text: `*ngIf` could not hold more than one element
choices.why: That limit was real, but it is not why `else` was separate.

choices.text: The old compiler read templates from the bottom up
choices.why: Templates were never read that way.

choices.text: To make the template faster to draw
choices.why: It was a consequence of the syntax, not an optimisation.

prompt: The control-flow migration turned `trackBy: byId` into `track byId(i, course)`. What does the lesson suggest doing with that?

choices.text: Nothing: the migration's output is the recommended form
choices.why: The lesson calls it correct and not what anybody would write today.

choices.text: Revert it, because `@for` cannot call a method in its track
choices.why: It can, and the migrated template worked.

choices.text: Write `track course.id` and delete the method
choices.why: Right. The same key, without the indirection.

choices.text: Add `NgFor` back to the imports so both forms work
choices.why: The new form needs no import, and nothing uses `NgFor` any more.

prompt: Put the steps the lesson took to migrate the bench in order.
items: write the template with `*ngIf` and `*ngFor`, and check it works
commit, so the migration's edits stand alone

prompt: A template must show `No sessions this week` when a list is empty and each session otherwise. Which construct does it with one block?

choices.text: `@if (list.length) { … } @else { … }` around an `@for`
choices.why: That works, with two constructs where one suffices.

choices.text: `@for` with an `@empty`
choices.why: Right. The empty case belongs to the loop.

choices.text: `@switch (list.length)` with a case for 0
choices.why: A switch on a count would need a case per number.

choices.text: `@let empty = true;`
choices.why: `@let` names a value; it does not repeat anything.
